R01-G-01: Governments that once judged their success almost entirely by output have lately begun to ask citizens a different question: all things considered, how satisfied are you with your life these days? The answers, usually given on a scale from zero to ten, are collected, averaged and compared across regions and years, and a rising average is increasingly cited as evidence that policy is working. The appeal of this approach is easy to understand. Income is at best a means to living well, and a measure that asks people directly about their lives seems to cut out the middleman. Yet the question is less direct than it looks. To answer it, a respondent must do something quite unlike reporting a sensation. She must call to mind her life as a whole, choose the standards by which it is to be judged, and compare the one with the other. The number she gives is therefore an evaluation, and evaluations depend on the standards brought to them. Two people whose days contain the same mixture of pleasure, worry and boredom may give very different scores because one expects more from life than the other. A person who has learned to expect little can report contentment with circumstances that would dismay a neighbour, and a population whose expectations rise quickly can report falling satisfaction even as its conditions improve. None of this makes the surveys worthless. Evaluations matter in their own right: how people judge their lives shapes what they choose, whom they blame and whether they think change is possible. The scores also move in ways we would expect, dropping when people lose their jobs or fall seriously ill. The error lies not in collecting the numbers but in treating them as a complete reading of how well people are living. A measure of judgement is not a measure of experience, and neither is it a measure of whether a life contains the goods, such as health, friendship and freedom, that most traditions of thought have held to be worth having whatever one happens to feel about them. A sensible policy, then, would treat satisfaction scores as one instrument among several, read alongside measures of how people actually spend and feel their days and of what they are really able to do. Used alone, the scores reward whatever lowers expectations as readily as whatever improves lives, and a government that steered by them alone could succeed by teaching its citizens to want less.
R01-G-02: The handbook of Epictetus's teachings opens with a distinction that has outlived nearly everything else in ancient ethics: some things are up to us and some are not. Our judgements, intentions and desires are up to us; our bodies, our possessions, our reputations and the offices we hold are not. In its modern popular form the distinction is offered as a technique for calm. Worry, it is said, comes from caring about what one cannot change, so the remedy is to stop caring about it, and the person who masters this will be undisturbed by traffic, criticism and bad news alike. This reading is not exactly wrong, but it inverts the order of the original argument. For the Stoics, tranquillity was a consequence, not the goal. The goal was to place one's good where it actually lay, in the quality of one's own choosing, and the distinction between what is and is not up to us was a claim about value before it was advice about feeling. To say that a friend's illness is not up to me is not to say that I should be indifferent to it; it is to say that my goodness as a person does not depend on whether she recovers, but on whether I act well toward her. The Stoic was expected to visit the sick, serve in public life and keep his promises with full seriousness, while declining to stake his worth on how any of it turned out. Read this way, the doctrine is more demanding than the popular version, not less. It asks for constant attention to one's own judgements, which the Stoics thought were the real source of most distress, and it offers no permission to withdraw. Someone who uses it to stop voting because elections are not up to him has learned a convenient half of the lesson and discarded the half that mattered. There is, however, a genuine difficulty that the more careful reading does not remove. The line between what is up to us and what is not is drawn more sharply in the doctrine than in life. Whether I pass an examination is not wholly up to me, but it is hardly independent of my effort; whether my child grows up kind is partly my doing and partly not. Most of what we care about lies in this middle region, and a doctrine that sorts everything into two bins must either treat such outcomes as indifferent, which seems false to how they matter, or admit that our worth is, after all, partly hostage to fortune. The Stoics chose the first answer. One can admire the clarity of that choice and still doubt that it describes a life anyone actually leads.
R01-G-03: Among the stories collected in the Zhuangzi, one of the best known concerns an enormous tree. A master carpenter passes it without a second glance, and when his apprentice asks why so magnificent a specimen has been ignored, he explains that its wood is good for nothing: boats made from it would sink, coffins would rot and tools would split. That night the tree appears to the carpenter in a dream and rebukes him, pointing out that trees bearing fruit are stripped and broken and never live out their natural years; its own uselessness, it explains, is precisely the reason it has lived so long and grown so large. The usual moral drawn from the story is a prudent one: in a dangerous world, conspicuous talent invites exploitation, and the wise keep their heads down. That reading has support in the text, which elsewhere praises figures who survive by escaping notice. But it makes the story smaller than it is. The carpenter's mistake is not merely that he underrates the tree; it is that he assumes the only question worth asking about a tree is what it is good for to a carpenter. The tree's reply amounts to the observation that usefulness is always usefulness to someone, for some purpose, and that a thing seen only through that lens is not really seen at all. This point has lost none of its edge. We are surrounded by institutions that measure things by their contribution to some further end, and we have grown skilled at the carpenter's glance. A subject of study is asked to justify itself by the jobs it leads to, a stretch of land by the revenue it can produce, an hour of a person's time by what it yields. Each of these questions is reasonable on its own, and institutions that never asked them would be failing in their responsibilities. What the story warns against is letting one of them become the only question, so that whatever cannot answer it, a friendship, a landscape, an afternoon of unhurried conversation, is passed by as if it were not there. It would be a mistake, though, to read the story as a rejection of usefulness as such. Boats and coffins must be made from something, and a world of nothing but magnificent useless trees would be a hard place to live. The story's target is narrower and more interesting: the habit of mind that cannot see a tree as anything other than timber not yet cut, and that mistakes the list of its own purposes for an inventory of what the world contains.
R01-G-04: Epicurus held that death is nothing to us, since where death is, we are not, and his Roman follower Lucretius added an argument that has been discussed ever since. Look back, Lucretius suggests, at the endless stretch of time that passed before you were born, which did not trouble you then and does not trouble you now. The time after your death is a mirror held up to that earlier time, and it would be inconsistent to dread the one while feeling nothing about the other. If non-existence before birth is no evil, non-existence after death can be none either. The argument has a pleasing economy, and against one target it is decisive. Many people who fear death picture it, half consciously, as a condition they will find themselves in: a darkness, a silence, an interminable wait. Against this picture the mirror works admirably: nobody imagines that they spent the centuries before their birth sitting patiently in the dark, and the comparison exposes the fear of being dead as a confusion, since there will be no one there to suffer the darkness. But most people who fear death are not chiefly afraid of a condition; they are afraid of losing what they would otherwise have had: the next conversation, the completion of their work, the sight of their children grown. Here the symmetry breaks down, because our attitudes to past and future are not symmetrical even in ordinary life; we look forward to pleasures and dread pains that are still to come in a way that has no counterpart for those already over. More importantly, the goods we stand to lose by dying are goods that this very life would have contained had it continued, whereas the goods of the centuries before our birth were never ours to lose. A person could hardly have been born a hundred years earlier and remained the same person, with the same parents and history; but the same person can very easily die later than he in fact does. This does not mean that Lucretius has nothing to teach. If the fear of death is partly a fear of a condition, then his argument removes part of the fear, and that is no small gift. What remains is better described as grief in advance for a life cut short, and grief of that kind is not a confusion to be argued away. It is the shadow cast by caring about one's own future, and a consolation that worked perfectly against it would have to work by teaching us to care less.
R01-G-05: On the eve of a battle, the Bhagavad Gita relates, the warrior Arjuna loses heart at the prospect of fighting his own kinsmen, and his charioteer Krishna answers him in a long discourse. One of its central teachings is that a person has a claim on his action but not on its fruits: he should act, and act well, without making the outcome the motive of what he does, and he should meet success and failure with the same evenness of mind. The teaching has been admired across many centuries and many traditions, and it has also been accused of something close to moral recklessness. An agent who does not care about outcomes, the objection runs, is an agent who will not count the cost of what he does. The objection rests on running together two different things: attending to consequences and depending on them. Nothing in the idea of acting without attachment forbids a person from considering what his action is likely to bring about; a physician who acts in this spirit still chooses the treatment most likely to help. What the teaching asks is that the physician's steadiness, and his sense of having done what he should, not be held hostage to whether the patient recovers. Consequences enter into deciding what to do. They do not enter into the agent's claim to a reward, or into the anxious craving that so often bends judgement toward whatever promises to be noticed and praised. Seen this way, detachment is less a withdrawal from the world than a condition for acting well in it. Anxiety about results is notoriously bad for performance; the craftsman watching the clock and the speaker imagining the applause both tend to do worse work than the one absorbed in the task. More seriously, an agent fixed on fruits is tempted to choose the action whose success will be visible over the one that is right, and to abandon a just course the moment it begins to fail. The teaching guards against both distortions. It would be too quick, however, to declare the tension dissolved. Consequences cannot be considered in choosing and then set aside entirely in acting, because most actions unfold over time and must be adjusted as their effects appear. The physician has to watch whether the treatment is working. What the teaching can sensibly ask is not blindness to results but a particular relation to them, in which they are information to be used rather than verdicts on one's worth. Whether that relation can be sustained by ordinary people under real pressure is a question the teaching poses rather than settles.
R01-G-06: Public discussion tends to treat time alone as a problem to be solved. Loneliness is described, rightly, as a source of real suffering, and the remedies proposed, from neighbourhood programmes to ever more ingenious ways of connecting online, share an assumption: that the less time a person spends unaccompanied, the better. On this view solitude and loneliness are a single condition seen from two angles, the first merely a polite name for the second. The assumption confuses a fact about circumstances with a fact about experience. Loneliness is the painful sense that one's connections are fewer or thinner than one needs; it can be felt in a crowded room, and some of its most persistent forms occur within marriages and among colleagues who see each other every day. Solitude is simply being alone, and its quality depends on what one brings to it. For someone who is lonely, an empty evening confirms a lack. For someone who is not, the same evening may be the only time in the week when attention is not divided, when a thought can be followed to its end, or when grief or pleasure can be felt without being performed for anyone. Many traditions have valued this second kind of aloneness. Hermits, monks and contemplatives have sought it deliberately, sometimes for years at a time, and periods of withdrawal into wilderness or retreat recur in the stories told about religious teachers in very different cultures. One need not share their aims to see the point they grasped: a person who can never bear his own company depends on others in a way that makes his relationships less free. Friendship is richer between people who could survive without it. This is not an argument for withdrawal. Solitude is good largely because it is chosen and because it comes to an end; a solitude imposed by exclusion, or one that stretches on with no prospect of return, turns into the very loneliness from which it was supposed to be distinct. Nor is the capacity to be alone a substitute for company; it is a companion skill to it. But if the two conditions really are distinct, then policies and technologies that aim only at reducing time spent alone may, without anyone intending it, crowd out a good that most people need in some measure and few are ever taught to use. The cure for loneliness is better connection, not the abolition of solitude.
R01-G-07: In ordinary speech leisure is what is left over when work is done. It is time off, and its value is usually explained by reference to the work it interrupts: we rest so that we can return refreshed, and an employer who grants generous holidays is said to be investing in productivity. Even our defences of free time tend to be framed in these terms. Leisure, on this picture, is the pause that makes the next effort possible, and a person who takes too much of it is quietly suspected of having failed at something. Aristotle saw the relation the other way round. In the Nicomachean Ethics he argues that we are busy in order to have leisure, much as we make war in order to have peace, and the Greek word for leisure, schole, is the ancestor of our word 'school'. Leisure in his sense was not rest or idleness. It was the condition of being free to engage in activities chosen for their own sake, of which he held contemplation to be the highest, though he also counted the cultivated enjoyment of music among its proper occupations. Amusement, by contrast, belonged with work. We need relaxation because we cannot labour continuously, and amusement provides it, so amusement exists for the sake of further activity rather than as an end in itself; to toil for the sake of amusement struck him as childish. The modern inversion has a consequence that is easy to miss. Once leisure is understood as recovery for the sake of work, it inherits the standards of work. Free time becomes something to be used well, which increasingly means used productively: hobbies are pursued for the skills they build, exercise for the stamina it sustains, even sleep for its effect on the next day's performance. The result is not merely that people have too little time off, though many do, but that the time they have is colonised by the logic it was supposed to interrupt. Aristotle would have recognised the pattern. A life organised entirely around work and the recovery it requires has, in his terms, no leisure at all, however many holidays it contains. The obvious objection is that Aristotle's leisure was a privilege resting on the labour of others. The citizens free for philosophy and politics were supported by slaves, by women whose sphere he confined to the household, and by labourers and artisans whom he considered unsuited to full citizenship in the best city. A conception of the good life that excludes most people from it can hardly serve as a model for a society in which nearly everyone must work. This objection is just, and it should not be softened. But it tells against the distribution of leisure in Aristotle's city, not against his account of what leisure is. One can reject the arrangement that gave a few men freedom from necessity while still holding that freedom from necessity is valuable for what it makes possible, and that what it makes possible is not simply more work. What follows for us is less a programme than a question. If the value of leisure lies in activities worth doing for their own sake, then the measure of a society's free time is not only how much of it there is but whether people have the means, the education and the settled habits to fill it with such activities, rather than with recovery alone. That is a demand on schools and cities as much as on employers, and it is one that the language of rest and productivity has no words to state.
R01-G-08: Few doctrines have been more often misunderstood by sympathetic outsiders than the Buddhist teaching of anatta, usually translated as 'no-self'. Stated baldly, as the claim that there is no self, it seems to invite an easy refutation: someone, after all, is entertaining the doctrine, and someone will be disappointed if it turns out to be false. Critics who press this point imagine that they have found a contradiction at the heart of the tradition. In fact they have mostly found a problem of translation, and behind it a mistaken assumption about what kind of claim the teaching was meant to be. In the early discourses the teaching typically appears not as a thesis about what exists but as an exercise. The listener is led through the components that make up a person, which the tradition groups as bodily form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness, and is asked of each whether it is permanent, whether it is reliably satisfying and whether it is under one's control. Since none of them passes these tests, none, the discourse concludes, should be regarded as 'mine', as what 'I am', or as 'my self'. The point of the exercise is practical. According to the tradition's own account of suffering, its origin lies in craving, and craving is sustained by the habit of treating changing and uncontrollable processes as possessions one must defend. To see that nothing in experience is fit to be owned in that way is to loosen the grip of the habit. Read in this light, the easy refutation misses its target. The teaching does not deny that there is a stream of experiences, nor that the stream has a history, makes choices and bears their consequences; the same tradition has a great deal to say about all three. What it denies is that there is, in addition to the stream, an unchanging owner standing behind it, and it denies this chiefly because belief in such an owner is what makes us cling. A later dialogue makes the point with a chariot: the word names an assembly of axle, wheels and frame, and nothing is lost by admitting that there is no further chariot over and above the parts, arranged as they are. The person, likewise, is a convenient name for a functioning whole, not a hidden thing to which the whole belongs. It would be too convenient, however, to conclude that the doctrine is purely therapeutic and therefore immune to philosophical scrutiny. A therapy that works by inducing a belief earns its authority only if the belief is warranted; otherwise it is a comforting fiction, and the tradition has never presented its teaching as a fiction. The exercise succeeds, by its own standards, because it reveals how things are. So the metaphysical question cannot be set aside; it can only be stated more precisely. The question is not whether anyone exists but whether a person is anything more than the organised stream, and on that question the doctrine takes a position that some philosophers in other traditions have also defended, and others have rejected, without anyone having settled the matter. The lesson for the sympathetic outsider is therefore double. The easy refutation fails, because it attacks a claim the teaching does not make. But the easy defence fails too, because the teaching is not merely a technique; it is a technique whose authority rests on a claim about the self that may be true or false, and that deserves to be argued about on its merits rather than admired from a respectful distance.
